title: Uniqueness with fixed prime-power local pinnings
statement: Let $\ell$ be a prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $T$ a Noetherian excellent scheme on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Fix a dimension function $\delta$ and use pinned potential dualizing complexes as in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. There exists such a complex for $(T,\delta,\Lambda)$. Any two such complexes admit a unique pinning-preserving isomorphism. Every such complex belongs to the bounded constructible etale category $D^b_c(T_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes] and has finite Tor amplitude, meaning that its derived tensor with an arbitrary module sheaf in degree zero has cohomology in a fixed finite interval [def-kun-derived-tensor]. Uniqueness refers to complexes with their pinnings, and does not assert uniqueness of unnormalized dualizing objects.

proof.text: For existence and uniqueness retain the stronger property that every pinned potential $K$ also satisfies $\Lambda_X\cong\tau_{\leq0}R\mathcal Hom(K,K)$. Reduction does not change this property: the reduction map is a universal homeomorphism, and its etale topos equivalence identifies constant coefficients, complexes, their cohomology, and derived Hom. It also identifies supported cohomology, since the complementary open and the kernel defining support correspond. The residue transitions defining potentiality use the same reduced curves and their normalizations after strict localization, hence the same pinnings and compatibility equations. Thus complexes and pinning-preserving morphisms correspond under reduction. The empty scheme has its zero complex and a singleton morphism set. It remains to prove the stronger property for reduced schemes.

source.place: XVII, 5.5, reduction to the reduced case; definitions 1.4.1 and 2.1.1-2.1.2

proof.text: For normal $X$, its finitely many normal integral components are open and closed. Work on one component, with generic point $\eta$, and put $m=\delta(\eta)$. Twisting by $\Lambda(-m)$ and shifting by $[-2m]$ changes each pinning to one for $\delta-m$, whose generic value is zero. The normal-extension lemma constructs $T=\tau^\varphi_{\leq0}Rj_*\Lambda$ with those pinnings, identifies every such normalized potential complex with $T$ by a unique pinned isomorphism, and gives its scalar derived-Hom rigidity. The twist-line lemma makes these twists locally free of rank one, so evaluation against their module duals is locally the identity and hence an isomorphism. Supported cohomology and its linear residue maps commute with such tensoring, as one checks on an etale cover trivializing the line. Twist back by $\Lambda(m)[2m]$; the two operations are inverse, so they preserve uniqueness and identify endomorphism complexes. Taking the finite disjoint union of these complexes gives the desired object on $X$; restrictions of sheaves, complexes, and morphisms to disjoint open-and-closed components are independent. Thus the stronger property holds on every normal $X$.

Use Noetherian induction on closed supports, strengthened to all schemes finite over the given closed subscheme. The empty support was settled in Step 1. For a reduced scheme $Z$ in this induction, normalization gives a finite surjection $p:Z'\to Z$ with $Z'$ normal and an isomorphism over a dense open $U$. Put $Y=(Z\setminus U)_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $Y'=Y\times_ZZ'$. Both $Y$ and $Y'$ are finite over $Y$, and their supports avoid the generic points of $Z$. In the strengthened induction over a fixed base, their images likewise avoid the generic points of its image: the finite closed-map lemma makes the boundary images closed; on affine charts, incomparability of primes for integral maps shows that a point above a minimal prime of the image must itself be minimal (a smaller prime would have the same contraction). Thus these boundary images are smaller closed supports and the induction hypothesis applies. All schemes remain Noetherian excellent by finite-type stability, and $\ell$ remains invertible. The dimension functions are the induced ones $\delta\circ f$ of the gluing lemma; finite maps are proper with finite residue extensions, so finite pullback shows that they are dimension functions. Step 2 gives the stronger property on $Z'$, and induction gives it on $Y,Y'$. Apply finite-modification pinned gluing to this square: its cone produces the pinned complex on $Z$, while its uniqueness and scalar-Hom assertions prove the stronger property for every potential complex on $Z$. Reduction from Step 1 treats any nonreduced finite schemes encountered. This closes the induction and proves existence and unique pinning-preserving isomorphisms on $T$.

source.place: XVII, 5.5, applying Proposition 5.4.1 to the normalization square

proof.text: Let $V$ be a nonempty connected Noetherian excellent regular scheme with $\ell$ invertible, $\delta$ a dimension function on $V$, and $c(x)=\dim\mathcal O_{V,x}$. We show $\delta=\delta(\eta)-c$, where $\eta$ is the generic point; $V$ is integral by clause (3) of the regular-normal remark. By the regular-unit lemma $-c$ is a dimension function, so $e=\delta+c$ satisfies $e(y)=e(x)$ at every immediate geometric specialization $\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar x$. Induct on $c(x)$. If $c(x)=0$, then $\mathcal O_{V,x}$ is a zero-dimensional domain, hence a field, so $x=\eta$. If $d=c(x)\geq1$, let $A$ be the strict henselization of $\mathcal O_{V,x}$ at a geometric point $\bar x$. Then $\dim A=d$, and the maximal ideal of $A$ is $\mathfrak m_xA$, so it is the only prime of $A$ above $\mathfrak m_x$. Take a chain $P_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq P_d$ of primes of $A$ and put $P=P_{d-1}$; maximality of $d$ gives $\dim A/P=1$. Let $\bar y$ be a geometric point of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ over $P$ and $y\in V$ its image. The reduced closure $V(P)$ of its image in $V_{(\bar x)}=\operatorname{Spec}A$ has dimension one, so $\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar x$ is immediate. As $P$ is not maximal, $y\neq x$, so $y$ is a proper generization of $x$; any chain of primes of $\mathcal O_{V,y}$ extends by $\mathfrak m_x$ in $\mathcal O_{V,x}$, hence $c(y)<c(x)$. By induction $e(x)=e(y)=e(\eta)=\delta(\eta)$.

source.place: XIV, 2.1, remark after Definition 2.1.8 (a difference of dimension functions is invariant under specializations); used implicitly in XVII, proof of Proposition 6.2.2.1 together with Proposition 2.4.4.1

proof.text: Now let $K$ be any potential complex. Prove bounded constructibility by Noetherian induction on its scheme, first making the reduction of Step 1. The regular locus is open by the J-2 clause of excellence and contains every generic point: a reduced local ring at a minimal prime is a field, hence regular. Choose this dense regular open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, with reduced complementary closed $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$. Potential pullback gives potential structures on $j^*K$ and $i^!K$; both maps are separated finite type and compactifiable (the open map factors through the identity proper map of $X$, so its exceptional pullback is the right adjoint $j^*$ of $j_!$; the closed map is proper, so its exceptional pullback is the right adjoint $i^!$ of $i_*$, as in the test below). Their dimension functions are restrictions of $\delta$. Regular schemes are normal, so the component decomposition gives finitely many open-and-closed connected regular components of $U$. On each such component with generic point $\eta$, Step 4 gives $\delta=\delta(\eta)-c$, so the regular-unit lemma makes $\Lambda(\delta(\eta))[2\delta(\eta)]$ potential for the restricted $\delta$. The uniqueness just proved identifies $j^*K$ with this twist and shift of the constant finite free sheaf, which is bounded constructible: the twist-line lemma makes its positive twists locally constant finite free, and dualizing a local free generator proves the same for negative twists. Induction gives bounded constructibility of $i^!K$ on the smaller closed support $Z$. The open-closed constructibility test therefore gives $K\in D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$. This argument works for every $n\geq1$, including $n=1$.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 6.2.2.1 using Lemma 6.2.2.2 and Proposition 2.4.4.1

proof.text: Take $k=\mathbf F_\ell$ and $K'=R\mathcal Hom_\Lambda(k_X,K)$. Coefficient coinduction gives potential pinnings on $K'$ for $(X,\delta,k)$ without assuming Tor finiteness. The $n=1$ case of Step 5 makes $K'$ bounded constructible, in particular bounded. Step 5 already made $K$ bounded over $\Lambda$. Apply the prime-power Hom/tensor criterion to this bounded $K$: its condition (iii) is exactly the boundedness of $K'$, so its condition (i) gives a single finite Tor interval valid for tensoring $K$ with every module sheaf in degree zero. This proves the final assertion without confusing derived coefficient coinduction with derived tensor reduction.

split_report.summary: Followed ILO XVII normalization gluing for existence and pinned uniqueness, separate Noetherian induction for constructibility, and coefficient coinduction plus the periodic Hom/tensor criterion for Tor finiteness. Six strictly supporting lemmas are left statement-only. Reused regular pinnings, finite exceptional pullback, reduction invariance, excellence stability, and normal-component decomposition. No statement change.
split_report.blueprint: Ancestor lem-per-artin-gabber-affine-curve, Proof Step 3: the finite coefficient normalized dualizing complex needed in the generic-duality model. Realizes the finer existence/uniqueness/constructibility/Tor input created in lem-per-finite-regular-reduction-dualizing.

tool_uses.why: Reduction is a universal homeomorphism, needed to compare the identical small etale theories; the perverse unit has no replacement.
Generic etale-topos invariance tool for reduction; no curve or finite-field restriction.
Regular implies normal, and Noetherian normal schemes have finitely many clopen integral components; these generic scheme facts let both inductions apply the componentwise source results.
Generic commutative-algebra stability of excellence under finite-type maps, ensuring the normalization-square schemes satisfy the source hypotheses.

Ordinary finite-coefficient Tate lines are etale locally free of rank one and flat over any scheme with the torsion order invertible; used to normalize generic shifts and verify constructibility, without changing the proof route.
Closedness of finite morphisms ensures the boundary images in the strengthened Noetherian induction are closed supports.
Incomparability shows points above generic points of the finite image are generic, ensuring a nowhere dense boundary has smaller closed image.

Generic commutative algebra: strict henselization preserves Krull dimension, used to find an immediate geometric generization when normalizing the dimension function on a regular component; no node of the unit gives it.
Generic commutative algebra: the maximal ideal of the strict henselization is the extended maximal ideal, so a non-maximal prime lies over a proper generization; no node of the unit gives it.
